chunks: Serpentining for bus synchronization. The question: What is serpentining? Why is it important for synchronization?
Serpentining means adding zig-zag length to a trace on purpose. In a bus, the receiver reads every data bit at the moment a clock or strobe edge arrives.
If some bits travel a shorter route, they arrive early and squeeze the time window. Adding length to the short traces makes all signals arrive together.
Think of runners in a relay who must all hand off at the same moment. If one runner has a shorter path, you make that runner take a winding route so everyone arrives together.
The winding must not bunch up, or runners on neighboring bends cut across to each other. So the bends need space between them.
The receiver samples on each rising clock edge. D0 changes well before the edge and stays valid after: lots of setup and hold margin.
D1 arrives late: it changes closer to the edge so setup margin shrinks.
D2 is so late that its transition (the x region) coincides with the sampling edge: setup violation, so the bit may be read wrong. Serpentining pulls D1 and D2 back toward D0.
Skew: the difference in arrival time between signals that should arrive together. Unit interval (UI): the time of one bit, equal to 1 divided by the data rate.
Setup and hold time: how long data must be stable before and after the sampling edge ("Setup and hold times (SI view)"). Propagation delay: time per unit length, about 5.
9 picoseconds per millimeter on outer-layer FR-4 traces. Speed-up: when tight meander legs couple, so the signal arrives earlier than the length suggests.
A signal moves at about 6 picoseconds per millimeter on FR-4. A trace that is 6 mm shorter than its neighbors arrives about 35 picoseconds early. At 3. 2 Gb/s a bit lasts 312.
5 picoseconds. Take away 150 picoseconds for setup and hold and 50 picoseconds for jitter, and 112. 5 picoseconds remains for all skew. That is roughly 19 mm of length.
So you add meanders until every trace is within that budget. That is the whole idea.
"Serpentining means adding zig-zag length to the shorter traces in a group so that all the signals arrive within the timing budget.
In a clocked bus the receiver samples data relative to a clock or strobe, so skew eats directly into setup and hold.
On FR-4 it's about 6 picoseconds per millimetre, so a few mm of mismatch is tens of ps.
I match delay rather than length, keep meander legs at least three or four trace widths apart to limit self-coupling, and place them near where the mismatch arises."
